newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign investment seen boosting India debt market.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment seen boosting India debt market.

text.p: Indian dealers and analysts on Friday said moves to open the debt market to foreign investors were a major step in its development, which could lead eventually to a drop in interest rates.
"It is a most welcome development," said R.H.Patil, managing director of India's National Stock Exchange (NSE), where electronic debt trading takes place.
"It will definitely help in developing the debt market."
Indian market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), said on Thursday it had permitted foreign institutions to invest in government securities.
Analysts said the opening up of the debt market to foreign investors was a logical consequence of an economic reforms programme that began in 1991.
The Indian government permitted foreign portfolio investment in Indian companies for the first time in 1993.
SEBI said it had already cleared three foreign debt funds worth $253 million. The firms are J. Henry Schroeder, Credit-Suisse and Chescor, it said.
NSE's Patil said the addition of new players would add depth to the market, increase trading volumes and improve liquidity.
"At the moment, the volume of trading is quite small," he said. "We need market-savvy players if the market is to develop."
Analysts said interest rates would come down over the long-term as securities' prices went up.
"As more funds flow in, the increased demand for securities will push up prices and bring down yields," said Aashish Pitale, debt research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec).
Liquidity would improve with more players in the market, he said. Foreign investment would be accompanied by more scientific methods of pricing securities, he said.
Pitale foresaw the move helping to develop the corporate debt market as well.
"This is very important," he said. "We have seen that in other south Asian countries, once foreign investors are comfortable with sovereign debt, they move into corporate debt."
Over a period of time, this would enable Indian firms to access funds at lower rates, Pitale said.
Traders felt the arrival of professionally-run foreign outfits would prompt local dealers to hone their own skills.
"Local traders will have to perk up," said a dealer at the Gilts Securities Trading Corporation of India.
"We should see finer rates and more trading once the foreigners come in."
